messages.subject: endotherm model conduction issue
messages.body_plain:
Dear NicheMapR users,

We've found an issue with the way conduction is implemented in the endoR and endoR_devel models and we are in the process of fixing it. Conduction is not on by default so this is only something to worry about if you are turning conduction on in the model. We'll let you know when we've fixed the problem but for now it's best to turn conduction off. Sorry for any bother this might have caused.

All the best,
Mike

Not quite but that is a priority for this year. Marko Jusup and I are refining exactly how to compute heat production from the DEB model and will then finalise a whole-life-cycle bird model. Mike

"The ectotherm model also has scope to estimate transient heat budgets, and thus stored heat, QS, but without thermoregulatory behaviour. These aspects of the model will be described elsewhere."

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: simulating pond temperatures
messages.body_plain:
Dear Dennis,

You can use the ectotherm mode or the microclimate model to simulate pond depths and temperatures, but in a bit of a kludgy way.

For the microclimate model approach, you simulate a clay-based substrate and put a multiplier on the rainfall to simulate a catchment. I've found this can predict pond depths extremely well for a shallow wetland - it captures both the rain input and the evaporation/seepage output mechanistically, but not the water temperature. To get a rough prediction of water temperature you can use the water-logged soil temperatures for different depths to get a rough estimate.

Alternatively you can use the 'container' model of the ectotherm model, which simulates an open-topped container either sitting on the surface (like a paddling pool) or sunk into the ground, and you can optionally put a hole in it (constant drainage per day) and vary the fraction of the surface that evaporates (to simulate it being partly covered). This can be computationally more intensive but will give a more accurate estimate of what the water temperature would be at the centre of the pond.

The main thing of course is to have some good data with which to test it. Down the track we may finish integrating the 'General Lake Model' with NicheMapR, which is a proper fully-physical model of a water body with stratification etc.

I’ve put some example code together (using the micro_usa function) below to show you how to implement the two approaches. Note the ectotherm model simulation took about 25 mins for the 2 year simulation! And also note that you'll have to install the latest version of the ectotherm model for the code below to work because there was a bug in the error trapping preventing 'conthole' from being different to zero or one, but it's fixed as of today.

All the best,
Mike

library(NicheMapR)

# microclimate model approach

# define textural soil properties for clay
soilpro <- matrix(data = 0, nrow = 6, ncol = 5)
colnames(soilpro) <- c('depth', 'blkdens', 'clay', 'silt', 'sand')
soilpro[,1] <- c(2.5, 7.5, 22.5, 45, 80, 150)
soilpro[,2] <- 1.4 # bulk density (Mg/m3)
soilpro[,3] <- 90 # % clay
soilpro[,4] <- 0.0 # % silt
soilpro[,5] <- 10 # % sand
DEP <- c(0, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 90, 200) # Soil nodes (cm)

# get hydraulic properties for given soil
soil.hydro <- pedotransfer(soilpro = as.data.frame(soilpro), DEP = DEP)
PE <- soil.hydro$PE
BB <- soil.hydro$BB
BD <- soil.hydro$BD
KS <- soil.hydro$KS
BulkDensity <- BD[seq(1, 19, 2)]

rainmult <- 4.5 # Rainfall multiplier to reflect catchment (1 will result in unadjusted rainfall)
maxpool <- 500 # maximium pooling depth (mm), i.e. wetland depth
LAI <- 0 # leaf area index (zero so no transpiration)
cap <- 0 # do not simulate the organic cap layer
soilgrids <- 0 # don't use SoilGrids soil database for thermal properties

micro <- micro_usa(PE = PE, BB = BB, BD = BD, KS = KS, rainmult = rainmult, maxpool = maxpool, LAI = LAI, cap = cap, soilgrids = soilgrids)
metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout)
soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil)
wetlandDepths<-as.data.frame(cbind(dates,as.data.frame(metout$POOLDEP)))
colnames(wetlandDepths) <- c('dates', 'pond depth')

# get closest soil depths for each wetland depth
depth <- apply(as.matrix(wetlandDepths$depth / 10), 1, function(x) which.min(abs(x - DEP)))
depth <- depth - 2 # actually choose 2 nodes shallower to better approximate amplitude
depth[depth <= 0] <- 1 # step above produces some values below one - correct this

# now get the soil temperatures for the corresponding wetland depths
wetlandTemps <- as.data.frame(as.numeric(soil[cbind(seq_along(depth + 3), depth + 3)]))
wetlandTemps <- cbind(dates, wetlandTemps) # append dates
colnames(wetlandTemps) <- c('dates', 'pond temperature')

par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(wetlandDepths, type = 'l', ylim = c(0, 500), main = 'microclimate model prediction')
plot(wetlandTemps, type = 'l', ylim = c(-20, 50))

# ectotherm model approach

# container model parameters
container <- 1 # Run the water body/container model? (aquatic start of life cycle, e.g. frog or mosquito)
conth <- 500 # Cylindrical container/pond height (mm)
contw <- 10000 # Cylindrical container/pond diameter (mm)
contype <- 1 # Is 'container' sitting on the surface, like a bucket (0) or sunk into the ground like a pond (1)
rainmult <- 4.5 # Rainfall multiplier to reflect catchment (1 will result in unadjusted rainfall)
continit <- 0 # Initial container water level (cm)
conthole <- 10 # Daily (or hourly if rainhr vector filled) loss of height (mm) due to 'hole' in container (e.g. infiltration to soil, drawdown from water tank)
contonly <- 1 # Just run the container model and quit?
contwet <- 100 # % of container surface acting as a free water exchanger

# run the ectotherm model (this is quite slow! ~ 25 mins)
ecto <- ectotherm(container = container, conth = conth, contw = contw, contype = contype,
                  rainmult = rainmult, continit = continit, conthole = conthole,
                  contonly = contonly, contwet = contwet)
environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
plot(micro$dates, environ$CONDEP, type = 'l', ylab = 'container depth', xlab = 'date', ylim = c(0, 500), main = 'ectotherm model prediction')
plot(micro$dates, environ$TC, type = 'l', ylab = 'water temperature', xlab = 'date', ylim = c(-20, 50))

messages.subject: Overheating Death
messages.body_plain:
Hey Mike,

I've been playing with the DEB and ectotherm software and I've noticed that no matter what I do I can't make a critter die through overheating or desiccation, even if I drop the critical thermal maximum, stick it in the middle of the desert (, and keep it from being able to burrow or find shade. The maximum body temperature in the yearsout table gets recorded as getting up to 50ish °C, which I would anticipate would be lethal for an animal with a critical thermal maximum of 35-40°C, but the animal itself just keeps on surviving year to year. I've tried it both with Eastern Water Skink from the DEB vignette and the Northern Pacific Rattlesnake Crotalus oreganus, which also appears in the add my pet database. Is that a problem on my end, where another parameter is allowing it to survive for some reason? (I'm using all the default options for the vignette other than those few changes listed above).

Also, could you clarify whether the critical thermal maximum in the parameter list refers to the temperature where the animal's body temperature reaches a lethal limit, or whether it's the moment where the animal goes into hyperthermia (and therefore still has a few more degrees it can withstand before it actually dies? I've seen the term used both ways in the literature and wasn't sure.

Thank you!
Adam

messages.subject: Re: Overheating Death
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

Thanks for pointing this out. I found the issue - I had prevented the body temperature in the DEB subroutines from rising above CT_max so that metabolic rates don't go crazy but the subsequent code in those routines that killed the animal above CT_max of course didn't work anymore. I've now corrected it and pushed it to github. Note that I've made it so it dies 2 deg C above CT_max rather than right on it. I might add in a lethal temperature as an extra parameter so that this isn't so arbitrary (but of course it depends on duration of exposure as well as temperature experienced so lethal temperature it is not a simple trait to define).

Re the desiccation issue, you need to set 'raindrink' to something greater than zero, otherwise they'll keep rehydrating as if they've got drinking water all the time (that parameter is the number of mm of rain that must fall in a day before they can be assumed to have ad libitum water). Had you set it greater than zero?

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: Operative temperatures at different heights
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julie,

To speed things up you could try downloading the NCEP data locally - there are details in previous conversations in this Google Group about it. But either way, you only need to run the microclimate model once, and then modify the microclimate inputs prior to running the ectotherm model. E.g. if you wanted to set local air temp to the 2 m reference value, you could do this:

micro$metout[, 3] <- micro$metout[, 4]

because column 3 is TALOC and column 4 is TAREF. You could do the same for wind speed and humidity, and for the shaded microclimate (shadmet) too. Note that by default the ectotherm model looks for e.g. micro$metout, micro$soil, micro$shadmet
as the microclimate inputs, just to make it easy to run so that you have less code to write. But you can pass it different, modified microclimate inputs, e.g. to set up a metabolic chamber example, as long as it's in the same tabular structure.

So I'd suggest you do something like this:

micro <- micro_ncep( ....)
ecto <- ectotherm( ...) # run the ectotherm model at the specified local height

micro_original <- micro # make a copy of the original version in case you need it
micro$metout[, 3] <- micro$metout[, 4]
micro$metout[, 5] <- micro$metout[, 5]  .... etc.
ecto <- ectotherm( ...) # run the ectotherm model using the modified micro output list

All the best,
Mike

I was indeed not setting raindrink to anything other than zero. That makes sense why they keep rehydrating! I do have a few follow up question about that, though.

1. Is the raindrink parameter compared to the climate data to see whether enough rain is falling?
2. Do you recommend finding the average yearly rainfall in a given location where the animal lives and dividing by the number of days in a year to get raindrink? Or should it be more of an estimation of how much water that the animal really needs and figuring out how much is available in the environment somehow?
3. How exactly does the model calculate whether the animal dehydrates when it doesn't have access to infinite water? Meaning, is there a foraging cost built in or something, so that it will still manage to get enough water but with more effort? Or will it just automatically die if it never rains enough to have water available ad libitum?

Adam

messages.subject: Re: Overheating Death
messages.body_plain:
Hi Adam,

Yes it looks at the daily rainfall vector (assumed to be micro$RAINFALL) and if it is above the 'raindrink' threshold on that day, the animal is assumed to be able to rehydrate. Other than this input, the water coming in is from the water in food and the water from metabolism, and losses are from nitrogenous waste (i.e. urine), faeces, respiration and cutaneous losses including from the eyes. Check out the following for more details:

Kearney, M. R., S. J. Simpson, D. Raubenheimer, and S. A. L. M. Kooijman. 2013. Balancing heat, water and nutrients under environmental change: a thermodynamic niche framework. Functional Ecology 27:950–966.
Kearney, M. R., S. L. Munns, D. Moore, M. Malishev, and C. M. Bull. 2018. Field tests of a general ectotherm niche model show how water can limit lizard activity and distribution. Ecological Monographs 88:672–693.
Pirtle, E. I., C. R. Tracy, and M. R. Kearney. 2019. Hydroregulation – a neglected behavioral response of lizards to climate change? Page in V. Bels and A. P. Russell, editors. Lizard Behavior: Evolutionary and Mechanistic Perspectives. CRC Press.

All the best,
Mike
